lesson.title: Breaking and Making: Estimating Reaction Enthalpy from Bonds Alone
lesson.summary: Because breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it, the enthalpy of a reaction can be estimated as the total bond enthalpy of bonds broken in the reactants minus the total bond enthalpy of bonds formed in the products.
lesson.body:
A chemical reaction, viewed at the level of bonds, is nothing more than some old bonds breaking and some new bonds forming. Breaking bonds in the reactants requires energy input, an endothermic cost equal to the sum of the bond enthalpies of every bond broken. Forming bonds in the products releases energy, an exothermic payout equal to the sum of the bond enthalpies of every bond formed. The net enthalpy of the reaction is the balance between these two: delta H is approximately equal to the sum of bond enthalpies broken minus the sum of bond enthalpies formed. If more energy is released forming the new bonds than was spent breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall, and if the reverse is true, it is endothermic overall. This is a direct extension of enthalpy of reaction from several chapters back, just estimated from a completely different data source, average bond enthalpies, rather than from tabulated formation enthalpies or calorimetry.

Applying this method requires knowing the actual structure of every reactant and product, since you need to count exactly which bonds and how many of each type are present. Let's estimate the enthalpy of the combustion of methane producing gas-phase water, CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2 H2O(g). On the reactant side, one mole of CH4 has four C-H bonds, and two moles of O2 each have one O=O double bond, so two O=O bonds total. Using typical tabulated average bond enthalpies, C-H is about 413 kJ/mol and O=O is about 495 kJ/mol: bonds broken = 4(413) + 2(495) = 1652 + 990 = 2642 kJ.

On the product side, one mole of CO2 has two C=O bonds (each commonly tabulated at about 799 kJ/mol for the specific C=O bond found in CO2), and two moles of H2O each have two O-H bonds, so four O-H bonds total (commonly tabulated at about 467 kJ/mol each): bonds formed = 2(799) + 4(467) = 1598 + 1868 = 3466 kJ.

The estimated reaction enthalpy is then bonds broken minus bonds formed: 2642 kJ - 3466 kJ = -824 kJ. The negative sign correctly predicts that this combustion is exothermic, which matches everyday experience with burning methane. Comparing this estimate to the experimentally known combustion enthalpy of methane forming gas-phase water, which is close to -802 kJ/mol, the bond enthalpy method is in the right neighborhood but off by roughly 20 kJ, about 3 percent. That gap is expected and instructive rather than a sign of an error: it exists precisely because the C-H, O=O, C=O, and O-H values used here are averages pulled from many different molecules, not the exact bond strengths present in these particular molecules, echoing the averaging caveat from the bond enthalpy chapter.

The practical value of this method is that it lets you estimate delta H for a reaction using nothing but a table of average bond enthalpies and a correct Lewis structure for every species involved, without needing measured formation enthalpies or a calorimeter at all. It will not replace Hess's law calculations or tabulated formation enthalpies when precision matters, but it is often the fastest way to get a reasonable estimate and, just as importantly, to build intuition for why a reaction releases or absorbs energy by looking directly at which bonds are stronger, the ones broken or the ones formed.
